 View Comments Representative Ayanna Pressley spoke during a get-out-the-vote rally for Massachusetts Democrats Monday night in Boston. 
 Danielle Parhizkaran/Globe Staff Standing on the sidewalk outside Santarpio’s Pizza in East Boston Tuesday, Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley eloquently argued that the blue wave expected in the 2026 elections wasn’t the result of short-term voter anger but rather had been a long time coming. 
 “Listen, 2026 is just like the change election year when I was elected to Congress for the first time,” Pressley observed. “I ran in 2018 on an agenda with many things, (including) Medicare for all, abolish ICE, cancel student debt, end qualified immunity. I was really an outlier, myself and some of my closest cohorts at that time. And we’ve just seen this movement multiply.” 
 Pressley had spent the closing stretch of the election campaigning across the South for candidates such as Angie Nixon, who was waging a surprisingly strong upstart US Senate campaign in Florida. 
 In the restaurant behind Pressley, local politicians were engaging in a 53-year-old political tradition, gathering for lunchtime pizza on Election Day. 
 The crowd was even more giddy than usual, flush with anticipation of a sweeping Democratic victory — and possibly, a mandate to finally challenge the policies of President Trump. 
 In matters closer to home, the action was all on the nine referendum questions on the ballot. Voters were to decide the fate of such questions as the future of the legal marijuana industry, whether the governor’s office and state Legislature should be subject to the state’s public records laws (absolutely!), and whether primary elections should become nonpartisan. 
 Those issues were all interesting. But let’s be real: The most pressing issue voters were deciding on Tuesday was who will run Washington. 
 And that, raises yet another huge question: If Democrats do regain control of the House and the Senate, what then? What will they do with that power? 
 Governor Maura Healey suggested that the focus in D.C. would now shift to issues that touch voters’ daily lives. 
 “Energy prices, electricity prices are going up in the South. Their housing prices are going up. People are losing health care,” Healey noted. 
 “I talk to colleagues all around the country, and people say they can’t afford gas, they can’t afford groceries, they can’t afford anything right now, and that’s why you see this turn, including in places that were historically Republican and voted for Trump. He’s just not done the job, and that’s what we have to do.” 
 We might not immediately know the outcome of races that will decide Senate control, including in Maine and Alaska. But there isn’t much doubt that voters have lost faith in the ability of Washington to solve their problems. 
 This isn’t just a matter of “anger.” Voters also seem to be feeling deep fatigue. Trump triumphed, in part, because he claimed to offer a solution to ineffective government. They want a government that delivers on its never-ending promises to make life better. Or at least more affordable. 
 Trump has failed at that, even in the view of some of his own supporters. But voters are still looking for the leaders who will deliver the relief they constantly promise. Even in deep-blue Massachusetts, where incumbents nearly all cruised to victory this election, you don’t have to look far to find the same restlessness that affects Americans elsewhere. 
 Pressley talked about her excitement at possibly having a Senate that will not relentlessly shut down the progressive ideas she and her allies have pushed for the better part of a decade. Though I’m not sure she meant it this way, it was a reminder that we’ve lived without a Congress that can do big things for a long time. 
 “The reason I’ve been really focused on the Senate as well is I want to make sure that after we use our power — because Democrats sometimes are afraid to use it — if we get the power, we have to actually use it and move meaningful legislation out of the House,” Pressley said. 
 “So many really meaningful, bold pieces of legislation that are essential both for repair, restoration, or reimagining. You know, I need people that are going to fight like hell and push leadership to take these votes up.” 
 Tuesday’s results held the promise of major reform. But the hard part, as always, will be fulfilling that promise. Winning on Election Day is just the beginning of turning the page on the crazy timeline we’ve been living in. 
 Adrian Walker is a Globe columnist. He can be reached at adrian.walker@globe.com . Follow him @Adrian_Walker .
